newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: FEATURE-Bangladesh despair linked to drinking water.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Bangladesh despair linked to drinking water.

text.p: Ibrahim Hossain is a worried man.
His wife often threatens to leave him -- not over any dispute or conflict but because five people in his family suffer from arsenic poisoning.

"Life has become somewhat tense ... my wife often says she can't live here any more. My problem is that I can't leave my family," said Hossain, who teaches zoology at a women's college at Rajarampur in the northwestern district of Chapainawabganj.
Like Hossain, despair is gripping many families in this village where people say they are fighting a losing battle against a previously unknown enemy.
As villagers drink water from wells considered safe, more and more people fall sick and develop various symptoms from black body spots to tumours and gangrene.
"We are helpless," said Mohammad Afzal.
Afzal, 26, believes he was infected by arsenic contamination years ago but only recently realised its dreadful effects.

"I rushed to doctors and specialists but to no avail. They themselves are not sure about how to deal with the problem," he said. "They did not prescribe medicine but only advised me not to drink from polluted wells."
Afzal lives in fear because one of his brothers has already died and several other members of his family have symptoms of arsenic poisoning.
WIDESPREAD CONTAMINATION
There is hardly a family in Rajarampur and nearby Nayansukha village which does not have at least one member suffering the effects of contaminated water.
"Fighting the effects of arsenic pollution is an uphill task and so far we have not had much success," said Dr Mushfique Ahmed, professor of Zoology and Mining at nearby Rajshahi University.
Ahmed and a few of his colleagues researching arsenic contamination say arsenic-related gangrene is usually the cause of death in victims.
"The problem is widespread. It requires coordinated efforts by researchers, doctors and the government to try to contain it," Ahmed said.

He said an arsenic content of up to 0.1 milligram per litre of water is considered safe for drinking, but in many areas in Chapainawabganj and neighbouring districts wells contained four or five milligrams per litre and sometimes even more.
Ahmed said some 10 million Bangladeshis were at risk of arsenic pollution.

"Contamination is caused by the (naturally occurring) arsenic-rich pyrite mineral in the water. Combating the problems is hampered by a lack of well-trained experts and inadequate research facilities," he said.
"Some victims suffer rotting of their nails, which is often mistaken as leprosy."
NO VISIBLE REMEDY
Public health authorities have sealed dozens of wells, including 15 in Rajarampur. But hundreds more are still in use because people have no alternative source of water.
River water is generally arsenic free but is often contaminated with other diseases.

"Hardly any progress has been made in the fight against arsenic pollution. In some of the worst cases, victims develop tumours in lower abdomen and die from bleeding when these burst," said Obaidul Huq Nantu, a front-runner in the campaign against arsenic contamination.
Himself a victim, Nantu says some 300,000 people in the Chapainawabganj area alone might be suffering from arsenic-related illnesses.
"Some people are aware that they have been infected but many are not. When they do become aware, it could be too late," he told Reuters during a recent visit to Rajarampur.
He said the public health department was doing little and had not attached much importance to what he called "a growing menace".
Ahmed said wells more than 50 or 60 feet deep were generally found to have high arsenic contents. "Those only 30 or 40 feet deep are usually safe," he said.

"We are trying to make the people aware of that," said Nantu, who works closely with the researchers. "(But) the government is virtually quiet (on the problem). Politicians tend to ignore it, the public health department is doing almost nothing and the general public are mostly ignorant."
DISASTROUS CONSEQUENCES
The government says only three people have died from arsenic-related illnesses over the past year.

But in a report earlier this year, Dhaka's Independent newspaper quoted health officials as saying arsenic contamination of sub-soil water threatened 15 million people in northern and southwestern Bangladesh.

A survey by a group of non-government organisations found many people in these areas had developed severe rashes, mainly on the palms of their hands and feet, and were suffering from chronic intestinal complications.
Doctors at a hospital in southwestern Chuadanga district said in February they had sought urgent help from the Health Department in Dhaka to deal with the growing problem of arsenic contamination.
Bangladesh's Health Minister Salahuddin Yusuf told a seminar in Dhaka that arsenic contamination in water was posing a "public health crisis".
Officials said hospitals had so far treated over 2,000 patients suffering from arsenic poisoning.
Doctors and officials say the social effects of arsenic contamination are as bad as, if not worse than, the health hazards.
"No groom would agree to marry a bride with arsenic poisoning -- except in very rare cases. These poor girls and their families face social rejection," said villager Mohammad Taheruddin.
"Some husbands have divorced their wives after they discovered symptoms of arsenic poisoning. Many others had their proposals of marriage refused," he told Reuters.
